question: Uber raised fares in some US cities, lifting drivers' pay per trip. Within a few months, what had happened to their hourly earnings?
options: Up roughly in line with fares
Down, as riders took fewer trips
answer: Back near where they started. Hall, Horton and Knoepfle found that after fare rises drivers worked more hours while riders took fewer trips, so each driver waited longer. Within about two months hourly earnings were back at their old level. The better rate per trip went on idle time: emptier cars, not richer drivers.
move: Where anyone can join, a better rate draws more people to share it.
ask: When my rate rises, who else joins to share it and what happens to my take?
trap: Assuming a higher rate per trip means more pay per hour.
reference: Hall, Horton & Knoepfle, Ride-Sharing Markets Re-Equilibrate, NBER Working Paper 30883, 2023
